goldens.comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.

The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.

The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/embeddable_host.rb:14 — URI#host drops the port while stored hosts retain it, so every configured host with a port is rejected despite passing validation.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/embeddable_host.rb, the validation regex on line 2 allows ports (:[0-9]{1,5}), and the before_validation strips the protocol and path but NOT the port. So a host like 'example.com:8080' would be stored. However, in record_for_host (line 9-16), it uses URI(host).host which returns just the hostname without the port. So if someone configures 'example.com:8080' and a request comes from 'http://example.com:8080/page', URI('http://example.com:8080/page').host returns 'example.com', but the database has 'example.com:8080', so the WHERE clause 'lower(host) = ?' with 'example.com' won't match 'example.com:8080'. This is a real bug where hosts with ports would never match.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb:24 — Interpolating each persisted host directly into an INSERT enables stored SQL injection when the migration runs

adjudication.rationale: The migration at line 24 uses string interpolation to insert the host value directly into SQL: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', ...)"`. The host values come from a site setting that was previously user-configurable. If a malicious value was stored (e.g., containing single quotes or SQL commands), it would be executed when the migration runs. This is a real SQL injection vulnerability in the migration code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/embeddable_host.rb:17 — Every embed authorization performs a case-folded database lookup with no matching index, forcing a full embeddable_hosts scan on a public request path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in app/models/embeddable_host.rb line 17, there's a query `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` that performs a case-insensitive lookup. The migration in db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb creates the table but does not add an index on the host column (or a functional index on lower(host)). This means every embed authorization will do a full table scan. While this is a valid performance concern for a public request path (embed_controller.rb calls EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?), it's not a bug per se - the code will work correctly, just potentially slowly at scale. This is an important architectural/performance concern introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/admin/embedding_controller.rb:18 — The embedding settings endpoint loads and serializes every host without pagination, so response memory and rendering cost grow without bound.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims there's a scalability issue with loading all embeddable hosts without pagination. However, looking at the diff, this is an admin-only endpoint for managing embedding settings. The number of embeddable hosts is expected to be very small (typically a handful of domains at most). This is not a realistic scalability concern - it's similar to loading site settings or other admin configuration. The finding is a theoretical concern that doesn't represent a real defect or important issue for this use case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/store.js.es6:197 — Every REST payload field ending in `_ids` is now required to be an array, so a valid nullable relationship from any existing endpoint crashes hydration with `null.map`.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff in store.js.es6 lines 192-210, the new code checks for fields ending in `_id(s?)$`. When `m[2]` is truthy (meaning the field ends in `_ids`), it directly calls `obj[k].map(...)`. If `obj[k]` is null (a nullable relationship), this will throw an error because you cannot call `.map()` on null. The code doesn't check if `obj[k]` is actually an array before calling map on it. This is a real bug that would crash hydration for any endpoint that returns a nullable `*_ids` field.

adjudication_records.issue_text: config/routes.rb:153 — Declaring the full `embeddable_hosts` resource publicly advertises GET index/show endpoints whose controller actions do not exist, causing those routes to fail instead of returning a supported resource representation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that GET index/show endpoints don't have controller actions, but looking at the diff, the EmbeddableHostsController (app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb) defines create, update, and destroy actions. The resources declaration in routes.rb for embeddable_hosts would generate routes for these actions. While index and show actions aren't explicitly defined in the controller, this is a standard Rails pattern where only needed actions are implemented. The routes are under AdminConstraint, so they're admin-only. The finding mischaracterizes this as a bug when it's actually intentional - only the needed CRUD operations (create, update, destroy) are implemented for the embeddable_hosts resource.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb:10 — Updating or deleting an unknown host ID dereferences nil and returns a server error instead of the API's expected not-found response.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb, the update and destroy methods use `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` which returns nil if no record is found. In update, `save_host(host)` is called with potentially nil host, which would cause a NoMethodError when trying to call `host.host = ...`. In destroy, `host.destroy` would similarly fail with NoMethodError on nil. The code doesn't check if the host exists before operating on it, so invalid IDs would cause server errors rather than proper 404 responses.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb:10 — Missing records are passed through or dereferenced, so stale update/delete requests raise a 500 instead of returning a controlled not-found response.

In destroy, `host.destroy` would similarly fail with NoMethodError if host is nil. This is a real bug - there's no nil check or proper 404 handling for missing records.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/admin/components/embeddable-host.js.es6:46 — Host deletion has no rejection handler, leaving failed deletes as silent unhandled promise rejections with no actionable feedback.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at line 46 in embeddable-host.js.es6, the delete action calls `this.get('host').destroyRecord().then(...)` but has no `.catch()` handler. While the save action at line 38 has `.catch(popupAjaxError)`, the delete action lacks error handling. This is a valid observation - if the delete fails, the promise rejection would be unhandled and the user would get no feedback. However, this is not a bug per se (the happy path works), but rather a missing error handling pattern that should be added for consistency and better UX.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb:11 — The migration dereferences the first embed_category query row before checking for absence, so installations without an overridden setting cannot migrate.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the migration code at line 11: `category_id = execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c...WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. This code accesses `[0]['id']` on the result of the query. If no row is returned (i.e., when there's no 'embed_category' setting or no matching category), accessing `[0]` on an empty result will return nil, and then calling `['id']` on nil will raise a NoMethodError. The code does check `if category_id == 0` afterward to fall back to uncategorized_category_id, but the error would occur before reaching that check. This is a real bug that would cause migrations to fail on installations without the embed_category setting configured.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb:25 — Legacy hosts are copied without URL normalization, so allowed values containing a scheme or path stop matching after the old settings are deleted.

adjudication.rationale: The migration at line 25 copies legacy hosts directly from the old site_settings value without normalization: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"`. However, the EmbeddableHost model has a before_validation callback that strips 'http://' and paths (lines 5-7 in embeddable_host.rb), and the host_allowed? method uses URI parsing to extract just the hostname for comparison. If legacy hosts contained schemes like 'http://example.com', they would be inserted as-is into the database, but the validation regex and matching logic expect just the hostname. The old SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host? method (now deleted) did handle stripping schemes with `.sub(/^https?\:\/\//, '')`, but the migration doesn't apply this normalization before inserting.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb:31 — Destructive setting deletion is embedded in a change migration with no reversible down path, so rollback cannot restore the prior configuration.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the migration at db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb uses `def change` but includes a destructive `DELETE FROM site_settings` statement on line 31. Rails migrations using `change` are expected to be reversible, but DELETE statements cannot be automatically reversed. If this migration needs to be rolled back, the deleted site_settings ('embeddable_hosts', 'embed_category') would be permanently lost with no way to restore them. This is a legitimate architectural concern about data migration safety, though it's not strictly a bug since the forward migration works correctly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb:11 — Migration dereferences the first embed_category row even when no override exists, so default installations can fail before deployment completes.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the migration code in db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb, line 11 executes a query to find category_id from embed_category site setting. The result is accessed with `[0]['id'].to_i` without checking if the result set is empty first. If no embed_category setting exists (which would be the case for default installations), `[0]` would return nil, and calling `['id']` on nil would raise a NoMethodError. The code does handle category_id == 0 on line 14-16, but the crash would occur before reaching that check.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb:25 — Migrated hosts are inserted without the model's normalization, so existing URL-form entries such as https://example.com silently stop matching after upgrade.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is valid. Looking at the migration (db/migrate/20150818190757_create_embeddable_hosts.rb), hosts are inserted directly from the old site_settings value without normalization: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"`. However, the EmbeddableHost model (app/models/embeddable_host.rb) has a before_validation callback that strips 'http://' and 'https://' prefixes and trailing paths. The host_allowed? method uses `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` where host is extracted from URI(url).host (just the domain). If old settings contained 'https://example.com', it would be inserted as-is, but lookups would search for 'example.com', causing a mismatch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/embeddable_host.rb:17 — Port-qualified hosts accepted by validation can never match because URI#host drops the request port while the stored value retains it.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real bug. Looking at the diff, the validation regex in embeddable_host.rb (line 2) allows ports: `/\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\/i`. The before_validation strips the protocol and path but NOT the port, so a host like 'example.com:8080' would be stored. However, in `record_for_host` (lines 10-17), `URI(host).host` is used which returns just the hostname without port (e.g., 'example.com'), and this is compared against the stored value which may include a port. This means a stored 'example.com:8080' would never match a lookup for 'http://example.com:8080/page' because URI#host returns 'example.com' not 'example.com:8080'.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/embeddable_host.rb:2 — Duplicate normalized hosts are allowed, making category selection depend on an unordered first row and silently routing embeds to an arbitrary category.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the EmbeddableHost model (app/models/embeddable_host.rb) has no uniqueness validation on the host field. Looking at the diff, line 2 shows only a format validation: `validates_format_of :host, :with => /\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i`. The `record_for_host` method uses `.first` to return a single record, and `EmbeddableHost.all.order(:host)` in the controller doesn't prevent duplicates. If duplicate hosts exist with different categories, the category selection becomes non-deterministic (depends on which record `.first` returns). This is a real defect in the data model design.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/embeddable_host.rb:6 — A create request with a missing or null host raises on sub! instead of returning a validation error, allowing malformed admin input to produce a 500.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is valid. In app/models/embeddable_host.rb lines 5-7, the before_validation callback calls `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` directly on the host attribute. If host is nil (missing or null), calling sub! on nil will raise a NoMethodError rather than allowing the validates_format_of validation to handle it gracefully. This would result in a 500 error instead of a proper validation error response.
